newsitem.title: USA: U.S. nonfinancial debt growth slowed in Q4.
newsitem.headline: U.S. nonfinancial debt growth slowed in Q4.

text.p: Total debt held by U.S. households, businesses and federal, state and local governments expanded at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.5 percent in the fourth quarter last year, the Federal Reserve said on Friday.
That was down from a revised 5.1 percent rate of increase in so-called nonfinancial debt during the third quarter last year, which was previously reported as a smaller 4.7 percent gain.
Nonfinancial debt represents borrowings by all economic sectors except banks, thrifts, finance companies and other financial services providers.
For the full year 1996, debt of domestic nonfinancial sectors grew at a 5.4 percent rate, down slightly from 5.5 percent in 1995.
The Fed said that growth of federal debt fell to 3.1 percent in the fourth quarter from 4.3 percent in the third quarter but at 4 percent for all of 1996 was little changed from a year earlier.

Growth of household debt declined in the fourth quarter to 5.6 percent -- the lowest for any quarter last year -- from 7.1 percent in the third quarter. "Both home mortgage borrowing and consumer credit moderated in the fourth quarter," the Fed said.
Household debt for all of 1996 grew 7.8 percent, down from 8.2 percent in 1995.
Business debt growth slowed to 3.6 percent in the fourth quarter from 5.9 percent in the third quarter and for the whole year eased down to 4.7 percent from 6 percent in 1995.
The Fed said that debt of state and local governments picked up to a 6.9 percent rate of growth in the fourth quarter after contracting by 5.7 percent in the third quarter.

Issuance of new municipal debt outpaced retirements of existing debts. The Fed added that for the full year 1996, state and local governments' debts grew by 1.2 percent after shrinking in the two previous years by 3.5 percent in 1995 and 3.4 percent in 1994.
At the end of 1996, there was a total $14.6 trillion of domestic nonfinancial debt outstanding, the Fed said.
